title: Ἄρης οὐτασμένος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Diomedes tells Athena he has recognised her, says he has held back as she bade him and drawn the Argives back because Ares is leading the fighting, and she answers that he must drive straight at Ares, a turncoat who promised to help the Argives and now keeps company with the Trojans. She thrusts Sthenelus down from the chariot, climbs in beside Diomedes, takes the whip and reins, and puts on the helmet of Hades so that Ares cannot see her. Ares leaves the Aetolian Periphas, whom he has just killed, and goes at Diomedes; Athena turns his spear aside, and Diomedes’ thrust, pressed home by Athena, wounds him in the lowest part of the flank. He bellows like ten thousand men and rises into heaven in a cloud, where he shows Zeus his deathless blood and complains of Athena and Diomedes. Zeus tells him that he is the most hateful of the gods and was born of Hera, but he has Paieon heal him; Hebe bathes and dresses him, and Hera and Athena go back to Zeus’ house.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: In answer strong Diomedes said to her:
sentences.n: Diomedes answers Athena, whose speech ended at 5.813. τὴν ‘her’ is the article used as a pronoun, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the aorist of πρόσφημι. The whole line is the ordinary formula for a reply, here with the stock epithet κρατερός ‘strong’ for Diomedes, and it is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκω σε θεὰ θύγατερ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.tr: gignōskō se thea thygater Dios aigiochoio·
sentences.l: “I recognise you, goddess, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.i: “I recognise you, goddess, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω with a person as its object is ‘I recognise’: Diomedes has understood who the helper at his side is. θεά and θύγατερ are both vocatives, and Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is ‘of aegis-bearing Zeus’, with the epic genitive in -οιο (= Attic -ου). αἰγίοχος is translated ‘aegis-bearing’ every time, though what the word first meant is disputed.

sentences.t: τώ τοι προφρονέως ἐρέω ἔπος οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr: tō toi prophroneōs ereō epos oud’ epikeusō.
sentences.l: so to you readily I will speak a word, and will not conceal it.
sentences.i: So I will readily say my word to you, and will not hide it.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore, so’, an old adverbial form of the article, and τοι is σοι ‘to you’. προφρονέως is ‘readily’, with a ready mind. ἐρέω is the future ‘I will speak’, and ἐπικεύσω the future of ἐπικεύθω ‘hide, conceal’; οὐδ’ is ‘and … not’, so the two verbs run together.

sentences.t:
οὔτέ τί με δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον οὔτέ τις ὄκνος,
ἀλλ’ ἔτι σέων μέμνημαι ἐφετμέων ἃς ἐπέτειλας·
sentences.tr:
oute ti me deos ischei akērion oute tis oknos,
all’ eti seōn memnēmai ephetmeōn has epeteilas·
sentences.l:
Neither does any fear hold me, spiritless, nor any hesitation,
but still I remember your commands, which you enjoined;
sentences.i: No spiritless fear has hold of me, nor any hesitation, but I still remember the commands that you laid on me;
sentences.n: δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον ‘spiritless fear holds’ gives Athena’s own words back to her: she had said δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον at 5.812. ὄκνος is ‘hesitation, shrinking’. σέων ‘your’ is a possessive in the genitive plural, agreeing with ἐφετμέων ‘commands’ (it is the uncontracted counterpart of Attic σῶν), and μέμνημαι ‘I remember’ takes the genitive. ἐπέτειλας is the aorist of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’.

sentences.t:
οὔ μ’ εἴας μακάρεσσι θεοῖς ἀντικρὺ μάχεσθαι
τοῖς ἄλλοις· ἀτὰρ εἴ κε Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη
ἔλθῃσ’ ἐς πόλεμον, τήν γ’ οὐτάμεν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
ou m’ eias makaressi theois antikry machesthai
tois allois· atar ei ke Dios thygatēr Aphroditē
elthēis’ es polemon, tēn g’ outamen oxeï chalkōi.
sentences.l:
You did not let me with the blessed gods head-on fight,
the others; but if the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite,
should come into the war, her at least wound with the sharp bronze.
sentences.i: You did not let me fight head-on with the other blessed gods; but if Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, should come into the war, wound her at least with the sharp bronze.
sentences.n: Diomedes now repeats the charge Athena laid on him at 5.129–132. εἴας is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, ‘you were not letting me’; μακάρεσσι θεοῖς is the epic dative plural, and ἀντικρύ ‘head-on’ goes with μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’. τοῖς ἄλλοις ‘the others’ is the article as a demonstrative, in apposition to the gods: all the gods except the one he names next. The last two lines are Athena’s own words at 5.131–132, given back to her, with the English of 5.131–132 in other order; ἀτὰρ εἴ κε … ἔλθῃσ’ is ‘but if … should come’ (εἰ κε with the subjunctive, for Attic ἐάν), and οὐτάμεν, the infinitive of οὐτάω ‘wound’, does the work of a command, with τήν γ’ ‘her at least’ in front of it. The quotation does not close here, for Diomedes’ speech goes on.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν αὐτός τ’ ἀναχάζομαι ἠδὲ καὶ ἄλλους
Ἀργείους ἐκέλευσα ἀλήμεναι ἐνθάδε πάντας·
sentences.tr:
touneka nyn autos t’ anachazomai ēde kai allous
Argeious ekeleusa alēmenai enthade pantas·
sentences.l:
For that reason now I myself draw back, and the others also,
the Argives, I ordered to crowd together here, all of them;
sentences.i: For that reason I am now drawing back myself, and I have ordered all the other Argives too to crowd together here;
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα (= τοῦ ἕνεκα) is ‘for that reason’: Diomedes has obeyed her command about the gods. αὐτός τ’ … ἠδὲ καὶ ἄλλους is ‘both I myself … and also the others’, with ἀναχάζομαι ‘I draw back’ in the present. ἐκέλευσα ‘I ordered’ takes the infinitive ἀλήμεναι and the accusative ἄλλους Ἀργείους πάντας. ἀλήμεναι is an aorist passive infinitive, ‘to be crowded together’, usually connected with εἴλω ‘press, crowd’, and ἐνθάδε is ‘here’.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκω γὰρ Ἄρηα μάχην ἀνὰ κοιρανέοντα.
sentences.tr: gignōskō gar Arēa machēn ana koiraneonta.
sentences.l: for I recognise Ares throughout the battle acting as ruler.”
sentences.i: for I recognise Ares ruling throughout the battle.”
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω now takes a participle: ‘I recognise Ares ruling’. κοιρανέοντα (accusative singular, agreeing with Ἄρηα) is the uncontracted participle of κοιρανέω ‘be lord, rule’, and μάχην ἀνά is ‘throughout the battle’, with the preposition after its noun. Diomedes’ speech ends here and Athena answers in the next line.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, answered him:
sentences.n: Athena replies. The line is the stock reply-formula for her: τὸν ‘him’ is the article as a pronoun, ἠμείβετ’ the elided imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and ἔπειτα ‘then’. γλαυκῶπις is translated ‘gleaming-eyed’ every time (the old explanation ‘owl-eyed’ is not sure).

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδη Διόμηδες ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ
μήτε σύ γ’ Ἄρηα τό γε δείδιθι μήτε τιν’ ἄλλον
ἀθανάτων, τοίη τοι ἐγὼν ἐπιτάρροθός εἰμι·
sentences.tr:
Tydeïdē Diomēdes emōi kecharismene thymōi
mēte sy g’ Arēa to ge deidithi mēte tin’ allon
athanatōn, toiē toi egōn epitarrothos eimi·
sentences.i: “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, dear to my heart, do not fear Ares on that account, you at least, nor any other of the immortals: such a helper am I to you;
sentences.n: Athena’s opening address is the same as Sthenelus’ to Diomedes at 5.243: Τυδεΐδη is the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’, and ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ ‘made welcome to my heart’ is the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι, here a vocative. μήτε … μήτε … ‘neither … nor’ carry the imperative δείδιθι ‘fear’ (a perfect-form imperative of δείδω); τό γε is ‘on that account’, in the accusative. τοίη … ἐπιτάρροθός εἰμι ‘such a helper am I’ puts in the present what she said of her help to Tydeus at 5.808 (where it was ἦα ‘I was’). Line 827 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the opening Ἄ of Ἄρηα, short by nature, counts as long and the ηα of Ἄρηα is run together into one syllable, with the γε before δείδιθι lengthened (the verb once began with a second consonant).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐπ’ Ἄρηϊ πρώτῳ ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους,
τύψον δὲ σχεδίην μηδ’ ἅζεο θοῦρον Ἄρηα
τοῦτον μαινόμενον, τυκτὸν κακόν, ἀλλοπρόσαλλον,
sentences.tr:
all’ ag’ ep’ Arēï prōtōi eche mōnychas hippous,
typson de schediēn mēd’ hazeo thouron Arēa
touton mainomenon, tykton kakon, alloprosallon,
sentences.l:
But come, at Ares first hold the solid-hoofed horses,
and strike at close quarters, and do not shrink from impetuous Ares,
this raving one, a fashioned evil, a side-changer,
sentences.i: But come, drive the solid-hoofed horses at Ares first, and strike him at close quarters, and do not shrink from impetuous Ares, this raving one, a fashioned evil, a changer of sides,
sentences.n: Three commands: ἔχε ‘hold, direct’ (imperative of ἔχω), τύψον ‘strike’ (aorist imperative of τύπτω) with σχεδίην ‘at close quarters’, and μηδ’ ἅζεο ‘do not shrink from, do not stand in awe of’. ἐπ’ Ἄρηϊ is ‘at Ares’ (epic dative) and μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ is the stock epithet of horses. In 831 μαινόμενον is ‘raving’, τυκτὸν κακόν is literally ‘a fashioned evil’ (τυκτός ‘made, wrought’, but how Athena means it is not certain), and ἀλλοπρόσαλλον ‘side-changing’ is built on ἄλλος ‘other’ and πρός ‘to’. The sentence runs six lines, so the unit is cut at the comma, and the relative clause that explains the last word begins the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὃς πρῴην μὲν ἐμοί τε καὶ Ἥρῃ στεῦτ’ ἀγορεύων
Τρωσὶ μαχήσεσθαι, ἀτὰρ Ἀργείοισιν ἀρήξειν,
νῦν δὲ μετὰ Τρώεσσιν ὁμιλεῖ, τῶν δὲ λέλασται.
sentences.tr:
hos prōiēn men emoi te kai Hērēi steut’ agoreuōn
Trōsi machēsesthai, atar Argeioisin arēxein,
nyn de meta Trōessin homilei, tōn de lelastai.
sentences.l:
who a while ago, on the one hand, to me and to Hera declared, speaking out,
that the Trojans he would fight, but the Argives he would help,
and now among the Trojans he keeps company, and has forgotten those things.”
sentences.i: who only lately, speaking out, declared to Hera and me that he would fight the Trojans and help the Argives; and now he keeps company with the Trojans, and has forgotten all that.”
sentences.n: Athena says what Ares has done. στεῦτ’ is the elided imperfect of στεῦται ‘declares, makes a solemn promise’, with ἀγορεύων ‘speaking out’; πρῴην is ‘a while ago’. μαχήσεσθαι takes the dative Τρωσί, the dative of the enemy (as κέλομαι Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι at 5.810), so Ares had promised to fight the Trojans, and ἀρήξειν ‘to help’ goes with Ἀργείοισιν. ὁμιλεῖ μετὰ Τρώεσσιν is ‘keeps company among the Trojans’. τῶν δὲ λέλασται ‘and has forgotten those’ uses the perfect of λανθάνομαι with the genitive, and the Greek does not say whether τῶν is his promises or the Argives. Athena’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φαμένη Σθένελον μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων ὦσε χαμᾶζε,
χειρὶ πάλιν ἐρύσασ’, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐμμαπέως ἀπόρουσεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phamenē Sthenelon men aph’ hippōn ōse chamaze,
cheiri palin erysas’, ho d’ ar’ emmapeōs aporousen·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, Sthenelus, on the one hand, from the horses she thrust to the ground,
with her hand drawing him back, and he then at once leapt away;
sentences.i: So saying, she pushed Sthenelus from the horses to the ground, drawing him back with her hand, and he sprang away at once;
sentences.n: Athena acts on her own advice. ὣς φαμένη is ‘so saying’; Σθένελον is the accusative of Sthenelus, who has been with Diomedes in the car. ἀφ’ ἵππων ‘from the horses’ stands for the chariot, ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, and χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’ (the -ζε ending marks direction). ἐρύσασ’ is the aorist participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, with πάλιν ‘back’. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Sthenelus, ἐμμαπέως ‘at once’ is a rare adverb of uncertain formation, and ἀπόρουσεν is the aorist of ἀπορούω ‘leap off’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐς δίφρον ἔβαινε παραὶ Διομήδεα δῖον
ἐμμεμαυῖα θεά·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ es diphron ebaine parai Diomēdea dion
emmemauia thea·
sentences.l:
And she stepped into the chariot, beside heavenly Diomedes,
eager, the goddess;
sentences.i: And she, eager, the goddess, got into the chariot beside heavenly Diomedes;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is ‘and she’, Athena, and ἔβαινε ‘was stepping’ is the imperfect of βαίνω, with ἐς δίφρον ‘into the chariot’; παραί is παρά ‘beside’, and Διομήδεα δῖον ‘heavenly Diomedes’ keeps the stock epithet. ἐμμεμαυῖα is the feminine perfect participle ‘eager’, put after the verb for emphasis, and θεά ‘the goddess’ follows it.

sentences.t:
μέγα δ’ ἔβραχε φήγινος ἄξων
βριθοσύνῃ· δεινὴν γὰρ ἄγεν θεὸν ἄνδρά τ’ ἄριστον.
sentences.tr:
mega d’ ebrache phēginos axōn
brithosynēi· deinēn gar agen theon andra t’ ariston.
sentences.l:
and loudly groaned the oaken axle
under the weight; for a fearsome goddess it carried, and a man, the best.
sentences.i: The oaken axle groaned loudly under the weight, for it carried a fearsome goddess and the best of men.
sentences.n: μέγα here is the adverb ‘loudly’, and ἔβραχε is a word for a loud harsh noise, here the groan of wood under strain. φήγινος is ‘of φηγός’, an oak (not the beech of the English name), and βριθοσύνῃ is the dative of cause, ‘by its weight’, from βρίθω ‘be heavy’. ἄγεν is the unaugmented imperfect ‘it carried’. δεινήν is feminine, which shows that θεόν here is a goddess, and ἄνδρα ἄριστον is ‘a man, the best’.

sentences.t: λάζετο δὲ μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: lazeto de mastiga kai hēnia Pallas Athēnē·
sentences.l: And took the whip and the reins Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: Pallas Athena took the whip and the reins;
sentences.n: λάζετο is the unaugmented imperfect of λάζομαι ‘take hold of’, with μάστιγα ‘whip’ and ἡνία ‘reins’. Athena now drives, and Diomedes is free to fight. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is her name with its stock second word.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ ἐπ’ Ἄρηϊ πρώτῳ ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.tr: autik’ ep’ Arēï prōtōi eche mōnychas hippous.
sentences.l: at once at Ares first she held the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: At once she drove the solid-hoofed horses at Ares first.
sentences.n: The line is 829 again, with αὐτίκ’ ‘at once’ for ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ‘but come’. ἔχε was an imperative there and is here an imperfect without the augment (= εἶχε), so Athena does at once what she told Diomedes to do, and the English repeats the words.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν Περίφαντα πελώριον ἐξενάριζεν
Αἰτωλῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστον Ὀχησίου ἀγλαὸν υἱόν·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ho men Periphanta pelōrion exenarizen
Aitōlōn och’ ariston Ochēsiou aglaon huion·
sentences.l:
Now he, on the one hand, Periphas, the huge, was despoiling,
of the Aetolians by far the best, Ochesius’ splendid son;
sentences.i: Now Ares, for his part, was stripping huge Periphas of his armour, by far the best of the Aetolians, the splendid son of Ochesius;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μὲν ‘now he, for his part’ is Ares, set against Athena in 844. Περίφαντα is the accusative of Periphas, an Aetolian fighter, and πελώριον ‘huge’ is his epithet. ἐξενάριζεν ‘was stripping (of the armour)’ is the imperfect of ἐξεναρίζω. Αἰτωλῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστον ‘by far the best of the Aetolians’ is a partitive genitive with ὄχα ‘by far’, and Ὀχησίου is the genitive of Ochesius.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν Ἄρης ἐνάριζε μιαιφόνος·
sentences.tr: ton men Arēs enarize miaiphonos·
sentences.l: Him, on the one hand, Ares was despoiling, blood-stained;
sentences.i: Blood-stained Ares was stripping him of his armour;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him, on the one hand’ takes up Periphas again, and ἐνάριζε is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω ‘despoil’. μιαιφόνος ‘blood-stained’ (μιαίνω ‘stain’ + φόνος ‘slaughter’) is Ares’ stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη
δῦν’ Ἄϊδος κυνέην, μή μιν ἴδοι ὄβριμος Ἄρης.
sentences.tr:
autar Athēnē
dyn’ Aïdos kyneēn, mē min idoi obrimos Arēs.
sentences.l:
but Athena
put on the helmet of Hades, lest mighty Ares should see her.
sentences.i: but Athena put on the helmet of Hades, so that mighty Ares should not see her.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη ‘but Athena’ answers τὸν μὲν Ἄρης. δῦν’ is the elided aorist of δύω ‘put on, go into’, without the augment, and Ἄϊδος is the genitive of Ἄϊς (= Ἅιδης), so Ἄϊδος κυνέην is ‘the helmet of Hades’. The purpose clause μή μιν ἴδοι ‘lest he see her’ (optative) shows what the helmet does: μιν is Athena, and ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ is Ares’ epithet here.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ ἴδε βροτολοιγὸς Ἄρης Διομήδεα δῖον,
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν Περίφαντα πελώριον αὐτόθ’ ἔασε
κεῖσθαι ὅθι πρῶτον κτείνων ἐξαίνυτο θυμόν,
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ ῥ’ ἰθὺς Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs de ide brotoloigos Arēs Diomēdea dion,
ētoi ho men Periphanta pelōrion autoth’ ease
keisthai hothi prōton kteinōn exainyto thymon,
autar ho bē rh’ ithys Diomēdeos hippodamoio.
sentences.l:
And when he saw, mortal-ruining Ares, heavenly Diomedes,
now he, on the one hand, Periphas, the huge, right there left
to lie where first, killing him, he had taken away his life,
but he went straight at Diomedes, horse-taming.
sentences.i: And when Ares, the ruin of mortals, saw heavenly Diomedes, he left huge Periphas lying right there, where he had first killed him and taken his life, and went straight at Diomedes, tamer of horses.
sentences.n: βροτολοιγός ‘mortal-ruining’ (βροτός ‘mortal’ + λοιγός ‘ruin’) is Ares’ stock epithet, and ἴδε is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω. The line 847 repeats the start of 842, ἤτοι ὃ μὲν Περίφαντα πελώριον. ἔασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘leave, let be’, κεῖσθαι ‘to lie’ follows it, and ἐξαίνυτο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐξαίνυμαι ‘take away’, with θυμόν ‘life’ as its object. βῆ ῥ’ ἰθύς is ‘went straight’, with the genitive Διομήδεος, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ is a stock epithet with the epic genitive -οιο.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
πρόσθεν Ἄρης ὠρέξαθ’ ὑπὲρ ζυγὸν ἡνία θ’ ἵππων
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ μεμαὼς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin iontes,
prosthen Arēs ōrexath’ hyper zygon hēnia th’ hippōn
encheï chalkeiōi memaōs apo thymon helesthai·
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, Ares was first to thrust over the yoke and the horses’ reins with his bronze spear, eager to take his life;
sentences.n: The first line is the line that opens the advance at 3.15, and its English is the same. πρόσθεν can mean ‘in front’ or ‘first’, and both are true here. ὠρέξαθ’ is the aorist middle of ὀρέγω ‘reach out’, so ‘thrust’ with ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ ‘with his bronze spear’; ὑπὲρ ζυγὸν ἡνία θ’ ἵππων is ‘over the yoke and the horses’ reins’. μεμαώς ‘eager’ is a perfect participle, and ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἑλέσθαι (tmesis) is ‘to take away his life’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τό γε χειρὶ λαβοῦσα θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
ὦσεν ὑπὲκ δίφροιο ἐτώσιον ἀϊχθῆναι.
sentences.tr:
kai to ge cheiri labousa thea glaukōpis Athēnē
ōsen hypek diphroio etōsion aïchthēnai.
sentences.l:
and that, with her hand taking it, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena
thrust out from under the chariot, to dart in vain.
sentences.i: And the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, took hold of it with her hand and thrust it out from under the chariot, to dart off in vain.
sentences.n: τό γε ‘that at least’ is Ares’ spear. λαβοῦσα is the aorist participle ‘taking’, and ὦσεν ‘thrust’ is the aorist of ὠθέω. ὑπὲκ δίφροιο is ‘out from under the chariot’; the picture is not wholly clear, but the point is that the thrust is turned aside. ἐτώσιον is ‘in vain’, and ἀϊχθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, so ‘to dart off in vain’.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖθ’ ὡρμᾶτο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ·
sentences.tr:
deuteros auth’ hōrmato boēn agathos Diomēdēs
encheï chalkeiōi·
sentences.l:
Second, in turn, rushed on Diomedes, good at the war-cry,
with his bronze spear;
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, rushed on second, in his turn, with his bronze spear;
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖθ’ is ‘second, in turn’, and ὡρμᾶτο is the imperfect of ὁρμάομαι ‘rush’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet, translated every time. ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ are the very words that begin 852, there for Ares’ spear.

sentences.t:
ἐπέρεισε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα ὅθι ζωννύσκετο μίτρῃ·
sentences.tr:
epereise de Pallas Athēnē
neiaton es keneōna hothi zōnnysketo mitrēi·
sentences.l:
and Pallas Athena pressed it on
to the lowest flank, where he used to gird himself with the belly-guard;
sentences.i: and Pallas Athena pressed it home into the lowest part of his flank, where he used to gird himself with his belly-guard;
sentences.n: ἐπέρεισε is the aorist of ἐπερείδω ‘press upon, lean on’, and the object is the spear, understood: Athena adds her weight to Diomedes’ thrust. νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα is ‘to the lowest part of the flank’ (κενεών is the soft part of the body between ribs and hip). ζωννύσκετο is an iterative imperfect of ζώννυμι ‘gird’, ‘used to gird himself’, and μίτρῃ is the dative of μίτρη, the belly-guard worn under the belt.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥά μιν οὖτα τυχών, διὰ δὲ χρόα καλὸν ἔδαψεν,
ἐκ δὲ δόρυ σπάσεν αὖτις·
sentences.tr:
tēi rha min outa tychōn, dia de chroa kalon edapsen,
ek de dory spasen autis·
sentences.l:
There then he wounded him, hitting the mark, and through the fair skin he tore,
and out the spear he drew again;
sentences.i: There he hit the mark and wounded him, and tore through his fair skin, and drew the spear out again;
sentences.n: Diomedes is still the subject. τῇ ‘there’ is the place where Athena pressed the spear; οὖτα is the unaugmented aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’, and τυχών the aorist participle of τυγχάνω ‘hit the mark’. διὰ … ἔδαψεν (tmesis) is ‘tore through’, from δάπτω ‘tear, rend’, with χρόα καλόν ‘fair skin’; ἐκ … σπάσεν (tmesis) is ‘drew out’, the unaugmented aorist of σπάω.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔβραχε χάλκεος Ἄρης
ὅσσόν τ’ ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι
ἀνέρες ἐν πολέμῳ ἔριδα ξυνάγοντες Ἄρηος.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ebrache chalkeos Arēs
hosson t’ enneachiloi epiachon ē dekachiloi
aneres en polemōi erida xynagontes Arēos.
sentences.l:
and he bellowed, bronze Ares,
as loud as nine-thousand or ten-thousand shout
men in war, joining the strife of Ares.
sentences.i: And Ares in bronze bellowed as loud as nine thousand or ten thousand men cry out in war, when they join in the strife of war.
sentences.n: The subject changes back to Ares (ὃ δ’). ἔβραχε is the verb used at 838 for the groaning axle, here ‘bellowed’, and χάλκεος Ἄρης is ‘bronze Ares’, a stock phrase. ὅσσον τ’ … is ‘as loud as’, and ἐννεάχιλοι and δεκάχιλοι are adjectives, ‘nine-thousand’ and ‘ten-thousand’, agreeing with ἀνέρες; ἐπίαχον is an aorist in a general statement (what men do whenever they fight). In ξυνάγοντες ἔριδα Ἄρηος ‘joining the strife of Ares’ the god’s name stands for war.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὸ τρόμος εἷλεν Ἀχαιούς τε Τρῶάς τε
δείσαντας·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ ar’ hypo tromos heilen Achaious te Trōas te
deisantas·
sentences.l:
And them then trembling seized from beneath, Achaeans and Trojans,
as they were afraid;
sentences.i: A trembling took hold of them, both Achaeans and Trojans, in their fear;
sentences.n: ὑπὸ … εἷλεν is split by tmesis, ‘seized from beneath’, with the subject τρόμος ‘trembling’ and the accusative τοὺς … Ἀχαιούς τε Τρῶάς τε ‘them, both Achaeans and Trojans’. δείσαντας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, ‘having been struck with fear’. The cry of Ares reaches both armies, and so the Trojans too tremble.

sentences.t: τόσον ἔβραχ’ Ἄρης ἆτος πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr: toson ebrach’ Arēs atos polemoio.
sentences.l: so loudly bellowed Ares, insatiate of war.
sentences.i: So loudly bellowed Ares, who never has enough of war.
sentences.n: τόσον ‘so loudly’ answers ὅσσον in 860. ἆτος ‘insatiate’ takes the genitive πολέμοιο ‘of war’, so ‘Ares, who never has enough of war’, the same epithet and the same English as at 5.388.

sentences.t:
οἵη δ’ ἐκ νεφέων ἐρεβεννὴ φαίνεται ἀὴρ
καύματος ἐξ ἀνέμοιο δυσαέος ὀρνυμένοιο,
τοῖος Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ χάλκεος Ἄρης
φαίνεθ’ ὁμοῦ νεφέεσσιν ἰὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν.
sentences.tr:
hoiē d’ ek nepheōn erebennē phainetai aēr
kaumatos ex anemoio dysaeos ornymenoio,
toios Tydeïdēi Diomēdeï chalkeos Arēs
phaineth’ homou nepheessin iōn eis ouranon euryn.
sentences.l:
Of the kind that out of the clouds a murky mist appears
after heat, when an ill-blowing wind is rising,
such to Tydeus’-son Diomedes bronze Ares
appeared, going together with the clouds into the wide heaven.
sentences.i: As a murky mist appears out of the clouds after heat, when an ill-blowing wind is rising, so Ares in bronze appeared to Diomedes, son of Tydeus, as he went up with the clouds into the wide heaven.
sentences.n: οἵη … τοῖος is the shape of a comparison, ‘of the kind that … such’. ἐρεβεννή is ‘murky’, and ἀήρ is the dark vapour or mist, not clear air. καύματος ἐξ is ‘after heat’, with ἐξ after its noun, and ἀνέμοιο δυσαέος ὀρνυμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘an ill-blowing wind rising’ (δυσαής ‘ill-blowing’, from δυσ- and ἄημι ‘blow’). Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ is the dative of the one who sees, and φαίνεθ’ the imperfect of φαίνομαι ‘appeared’. ὁμοῦ νεφέεσσιν is ‘together with the clouds’, and οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘the wide heaven’.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἵκανε θεῶν ἕδος αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον,
πὰρ δὲ Διὶ Κρονίωνι καθέζετο θυμὸν ἀχεύων,
δεῖξεν δ’ ἄμβροτον αἷμα καταρρέον ἐξ ὠτειλῆς,
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
karpalimōs d’ hikane theōn hedos aipyn Olympon,
par de Dii Kroniōni kathezeto thymon acheuōn,
deixen d’ ambroton haima katarreon ex ōteilēs,
kai rh’ olophyromenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And swiftly he reached the seat of the gods, steep Olympus,
and beside Zeus, the son of Cronus, sat down, grieving in heart,
and showed the deathless blood flowing down from the wound,
and so, lamenting, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And swiftly he reached the seat of the gods, steep Olympus, and sat down beside Zeus, the son of Cronus, grieving at heart, and showed the deathless blood running down from the wound; and, lamenting, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: The subject is Ares, carried over from the simile. ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘reach’, and θεῶν ἕδος ‘the seat of the gods’ is glossed by αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον ‘steep Olympus’. Διὶ Κρονίωνι is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’ (Κρονίων is a patronymic), with πὰρ … καθέζετο ‘sat down beside’. θυμὸν ἀχεύων is ‘grieving at heart’, with θυμόν an accusative of respect; δεῖξεν is the unaugmented aorist of δείκνυμι ‘show’; ἄμβροτον αἷμα is ‘deathless blood’, and ὠτειλῆς the genitive of ὠτειλή ‘wound’. The last line is the usual way of introducing a speech. The sentence runs four lines, and is kept as one unit.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ οὐ νεμεσίζῃ ὁρῶν τάδε καρτερὰ ἔργα;
sentences.tr: Zeu pater ou nemesizēi horōn tade kartera erga;
sentences.l: “Father Zeus, do you not feel resentment, seeing these mighty deeds?
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, do you feel no resentment at seeing these mighty deeds?
sentences.n: Ares speaks, and starts with the words Hera used to Zeus at 5.757, Ζεῦ πάτερ οὐ νεμεσίζῃ … τάδε καρτερὰ ἔργα; there the deeds were Ares’, and now he uses them of Athena and Diomedes. Ζεῦ πάτερ is the vocative ‘Father Zeus’, and νεμεσίζῃ the second person of νεμεσίζομαι ‘feel resentment’, with the participle ὁρῶν ‘seeing’ and καρτερά ‘mighty’ (the same word is ‘mighty’ at 757).

sentences.t:
αἰεί τοι ῥίγιστα θεοὶ τετληότες εἰμὲν
ἀλλήλων ἰότητι, χάριν ἄνδρεσσι φέροντες.
sentences.tr:
aiei toi rhigista theoi tetlēotes eimen
allēlōn iotēti, charin andressi pherontes.
sentences.l:
Always, you see, most dreadful things we gods have endured
by one another’s will, bringing a favour to men.
sentences.i: We gods have always endured the most dreadful things through one another’s will, as we bring a favour to men.
sentences.n: τοι is ‘you see’ (it began as σοι ‘to you’). ῥίγιστα is a superlative, ‘the most dreadful things’, and its exact derivation is not certain. τετληότες εἰμέν is a perfect participle with the epic εἰμέν ‘we are’ (= ἐσμέν), so ‘we have endured’. ἀλλήλων ἰότητι is ‘by one another’s will’ (ἰότης ‘will’), and χάριν ἄνδρεσσι φέροντες ‘bringing a favour to men’ gives the cause: each god favours his own side among men, and the gods suffer from each other for it. ἄνδρεσσι is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t: σοὶ πάντες μαχόμεσθα·
sentences.tr: soi pantes machomestha·
sentences.l: Against you we all fight;
sentences.i: We all fight against you;
sentences.n: μαχόμεσθα is the epic first person plural (= μαχόμεθα). The dative σοί after μάχομαι names the opponent, ‘against you’, a strong word for the gods’ quarrels with Zeus; the reason is given in the next unit.

sentences.t:
σὺ γὰρ τέκες ἄφρονα κούρην
οὐλομένην, ᾗ τ’ αἰὲν ἀήσυλα ἔργα μέμηλεν.
sentences.tr:
sy gar tekes aphrona kourēn
oulomenēn, hēi t’ aien aēsyla erga memēlen.
sentences.l:
for you begot a senseless girl,
a ruinous one, to whom always lawless deeds are a care.
sentences.i: for you begot a senseless girl, a ruinous one, whose care is always for lawless deeds.
sentences.n: τέκες is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω ‘bring forth’; the girl is Athena, and Ares does not name her. οὐλομένην ‘ruinous’ is the word that describes the wrath at 1.2. ᾗ is the relative in the dative, ‘to whom’, with τ’ (epic τε), and μέμηλεν is the perfect of μέλω, ‘is a care’, with ἀήσυλα ἔργα ‘lawless deeds’ as its subject. The sense of ἀήσυλος is not certain; ‘lawless’ is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μὲν γὰρ πάντες ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ
σοί τ’ ἐπιπείθονται καὶ δεδμήμεσθα ἕκαστος·
sentences.tr:
alloi men gar pantes hosoi theoi eis’ en Olympōi
soi t’ epipeithontai kai dedmēmestha hekastos·
sentences.l:
For the others, all as many as are gods in Olympus,
both obey you, and we have been subdued, each one;
sentences.i: For all the others, every god there is on Olympus, obey you, and each one of us has been made subject to you;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι … πάντες ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ is ‘all the others, as many as are gods’ (εἰσ’ is εἰσί), and ἐπιπείθονται is ‘obey’, with the dative σοί. δεδμήμεσθα is the first person plural perfect passive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’; the sentence slips from ‘they’ to ‘we’, and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ includes Ares among those who have been brought under Zeus.

sentences.t:
ταύτην δ’ οὔτ’ ἔπεϊ προτιβάλλεαι οὔτέ τι ἔργῳ,
ἀλλ’ ἀνιεῖς, ἐπεὶ αὐτὸς ἐγείναο παῖδ’ ἀΐδηλον·
sentences.tr:
tautēn d’ out’ epeï protiballeai oute ti ergōi,
all’ anieis, epei autos egeinao paid’ aïdēlon·
sentences.l:
but her neither with a word do you assail nor at all with a deed,
but you let her loose, since you yourself begot a destroying child;
sentences.i: But her you assail neither with a word nor with any deed; you let her loose, because you yourself fathered a destructive child;
sentences.n: ταύτην ‘her’ is the girl. προτιβάλλεαι is the second person of the middle of προτιβάλλω (= προσβάλλω), ‘you assail’, with ἔπεϊ ‘with a word’ and ἔργῳ ‘with a deed’; the verb is rare and the sense here is not certain. ἀνιεῖς is from ἀνίημι ‘let go, let loose’; the same verb means ‘urge on’ in 882. ἐγείναο is the aorist of γείνομαι, said of a father, ‘begot’, and ἀΐδηλον is ‘destroying’ (the word is also taken to mean ‘unseen’, and the sense ‘destroying’ is followed).

sentences.t:
ἣ νῦν Τυδέος υἱὸν ὑπερφίαλον Διομήδεα
μαργαίνειν ἀνέηκεν ἐπ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
hē nyn Tydeos huion hyperphialon Diomēdea
margainein aneēken ep’ athanatoisi theoisi.
sentences.l:
She now the son of Tydeus, overweening Diomedes,
has urged on to rage against the immortal gods.
sentences.i: She has now urged Diomedes, the overweening son of Tydeus, to rage against the immortal gods.
sentences.n: ἣ νῦν ‘she now’ is Athena, taken up from the last word of 880. ἀνέηκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι, which with an infinitive means ‘urge on’ (the same verb as ἀνιεῖς in 880). ὑπερφίαλον is ‘overweening’ and agrees with Διομήδεα, and μαργαίνειν is ‘to rage’ (from μάργος ‘mad’), with ἐπ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι ‘against the immortal gods’.

sentences.t:
Κύπριδα μὲν πρῶτον σχεδὸν οὔτασε χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ αὐτῷ μοι ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος·
sentences.tr:
Kyprida men prōton schedon outase cheir’ epi karpōi,
autar epeit’ autōi moi epessyto daimoni isos·
sentences.l:
Cypris, on the one hand, first at close quarters he wounded, the hand at the wrist,
but then upon me myself he rushed, equal to a divinity;
sentences.i: He wounded Cypris first, at close quarters, in the hand at the wrist, and then he rushed upon me myself, like a divinity;
sentences.n: These two lines are the same as 5.458–459, where Apollo says them to Ares, but the speaker’s ‘me myself’ is Ares here, and the English is as there, except that the quotation does not close. In 883 Κύπριδα is the accusative of Κύπρις ‘Cypris’ (Aphrodite), πρῶτον ‘first’ is the adverb (there spelled πρῶτα), and χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ ‘the hand at the wrist’ gives the place of the wound. ἐπέσσυτο is the aorist of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush upon’, and δαίμονι ἶσος ‘equal to a divinity’ is the phrase used of Diomedes at 5.438 and 5.459.

sentences.t: ἀλλά μ’ ὑπήνεικαν ταχέες πόδες·
sentences.tr: alla m’ hypēneikan tachees podes·
sentences.l: but me bore away swift feet;
sentences.i: But my swift feet bore me away;
sentences.n: ὑπήνεικαν is the aorist (third person plural) of ὑποφέρω ‘carry off from under’, with μ’ = με and the subject ταχέες πόδες ‘swift feet’, the epic nominative plural in -ες. Ares says that it was his own speed that saved him.

sentences.t:
ἦ τέ κε δηρὸν
αὐτοῦ πήματ’ ἔπασχον ἐν αἰνῇσιν νεκάδεσσιν,
ἤ κε ζὼς ἀμενηνὸς ἔα χαλκοῖο τυπῇσι.
sentences.tr:
ē te ke dēron
autou pēmat’ epaschon en ainēisin nekadessin,
ē ke zōs amenēnos ea chalkoio typēisi.
sentences.l:
truly for a long time
there I should have suffered woes among dreadful heaps of dead,
or else, alive, I should have been powerless from the blows of bronze.”
sentences.i: Truly I should have suffered woes there for a long time among the dreadful heaps of dead, or else been alive but powerless from the blows of bronze.”
sentences.n: ἦ τέ κε … ἔπασχον is a past condition left unfulfilled: κε with the imperfect, ‘I should have been suffering’. δηρόν is ‘for a long time’, αὐτοῦ ‘there, on the spot’, and ἐν αἰνῇσιν νεκάδεσσιν ‘among dreadful heaps of dead’ (νεκάς ‘heap of corpses’, with the epic dative plural). In ἤ κε ζὼς ἀμενηνὸς ἔα, ζώς is the Ionic form of ζωός ‘alive’, ἀμενηνός ‘powerless’, and ἔα the epic imperfect ‘I was’ (= ἦν); χαλκοῖο τυπῇσι is ‘from the blows of bronze’. Ares’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς.
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus.
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: Then Zeus who gathers the clouds, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: Zeus replies. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking with a scowl’ (ὑπόδρα ‘from under the brows’), the look that comes before sharp words, and νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’ has the epic nominative in -α. The edition ends the line with a full stop, but the speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t: μή τί μοι ἀλλοπρόσαλλε παρεζόμενος μινύριζε.
sentences.tr: mē ti moi alloprosalle parezomenos minyrize.
sentences.l: “Do not at all to me, side-changer, sitting beside me, moan low.
sentences.i: “Do not sit beside me moaning softly, you changer of sides.
sentences.n: μή τί μοι … μινύριζε is a prohibition, ‘do not at all … moan’, with μοι ‘to me’ and the present imperative of μινυρίζω, a low continuous sound. Zeus uses the word Athena used of Ares at 831, ἀλλοπρόσαλλε (here a vocative), and παρεζόμενος is ‘sitting beside’.

sentences.t: ἔχθιστος δέ μοί ἐσσι θεῶν οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν·
sentences.tr: echthistos de moi essi theōn hoi Olympon echousin·
sentences.l: Most hateful to me you are of the gods who hold Olympus;
sentences.i: To me you are the most hateful of the gods who hold Olympus;
sentences.n: ἔχθιστος is the superlative of ἐχθρός ‘hateful’, μοί ‘to me’, and θεῶν οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν is a partitive genitive with a relative clause, ‘of the gods who hold Olympus’. The line is nearly Agamemnon’s to Achilles at 1.176.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γάρ τοι ἔρις τε φίλη πόλεμοί τε μάχαι τε.
sentences.tr: aiei gar toi eris te philē polemoi te machai te.
sentences.l: for always strife is dear to you, and wars and battles;
sentences.i: for strife is always dear to you, and wars and battles;
sentences.n: The line is Agamemnon’s to Achilles at 1.177, and the English is the same as there. φίλη is singular and agrees with ἔρις alone, though it serves all three nouns, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’ here.

sentences.t:
μητρός τοι μένος ἐστὶν ἀάσχετον οὐκ ἐπιεικτὸν
Ἥρης·
sentences.tr:
mētros toi menos estin aascheton ouk epieikton
Hērēs·
sentences.l:
Your mother’s might, you see, is unrestrainable, not yielding,
Hera’s;
sentences.i: The might of your mother Hera is unrestrainable and unyielding;
sentences.n: μητρός τοι μένος is ‘your mother’s might, you see’, and the mother is named only in the next word, Ἥρης, in apposition. μένος is ‘might’, ἀάσχετον ‘not to be held back’ (ἀ- + a form of ἔχω; ‘unbearable’ is another reading), and οὐκ ἐπιεικτόν ‘not yielding’.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν ἐγὼ σπουδῇ δάμνημ’ ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.tr: tēn men egō spoudēi damnēm’ epeessi·
sentences.l: her, on the one hand, I with difficulty subdue with words;
sentences.i: I subdue her with difficulty, by words;
sentences.n: τὴν μέν ‘her, on the one hand’ is Hera. σπουδῇ is ‘with difficulty’ (it can also mean ‘in haste’), δάμνημ’ is the elided present of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, and ἐπέεσσι is the uncontracted dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’.

sentences.t: τώ σ’ ὀΐω κείνης τάδε πάσχειν ἐννεσίῃσιν.
sentences.tr: tō s’ oïō keinēs tade paschein ennesiēisin.
sentences.l: therefore I suspect you suffer these things through her promptings.
sentences.i: And so I suspect you suffer this at her prompting.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore’ (as at 816), and ὀΐω is ‘I suspect’, with the accusative σ’ (σε) and the infinitive πάσχειν ‘suffer’. κείνης is the Ionic ‘that woman’s’ (= ἐκείνης), and ἐννεσίῃσιν is the epic dative plural of ἐννεσίη ‘prompting’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ μάν σ’ ἔτι δηρὸν ἀνέξομαι ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα·
sentences.tr: all’ ou man s’ eti dēron anexomai alge’ echonta·
sentences.l: But indeed not much longer will I endure you, having pains;
sentences.i: But I will not put up with you much longer, beset by pains;
sentences.n: οὐ μάν is ‘assuredly not’ (μάν is an emphatic particle), and ἔτι δηρόν ‘any longer, for long’. ἀνέξομαι is the future of ἀνέχομαι ‘endure, put up with’, with the accusative σ’ and the participle ἔχοντα, so ‘put up with you while you have pains’; ἄλγε’ is the elided ἄλγεα.

sentences.t: ἐκ γὰρ ἐμεῦ γένος ἐσσί, ἐμοὶ δέ σε γείνατο μήτηρ·
sentences.tr: ek gar emeu genos essi, emoi de se geinato mētēr·
sentences.l: for from me you are the offspring, and to me bore you your mother;
sentences.i: for you are my offspring, and it was to me that your mother bore you;
sentences.n: γένος is ‘offspring’, with ἐξ ἐμεῦ ‘from me’, and ἐσσί is the epic ‘you are’. γείνατο is the aorist of γείνομαι, said of the mother, ‘bore’, and ἐμοί ‘to me’ is the father’s share in the child.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τευ ἐξ ἄλλου γε θεῶν γένευ ὧδ’ ἀΐδηλος
καί κεν δὴ πάλαι ἦσθα ἐνέρτερος Οὐρανιώνων.
sentences.tr:
ei de teu ex allou ge theōn geneu hōd’ aïdēlos
kai ken dē palai ēstha enerteros Ouraniōnōn.
sentences.l:
but if from any other of the gods you had been born so destructive,
then indeed long ago you would have been lower than the sons of Uranus.”
sentences.i: But if you had been born of any other of the gods, and so destructive, you would long ago have been lower than the sons of Uranus.”
sentences.n: εἰ … γένευ is ‘if you had been born’ (γένευ is the epic aorist of γίγνομαι), and τευ is τινος ‘any’, with ἐξ ἄλλου … θεῶν ‘from another of the gods’. καί κεν … ἦσθα is the matching ‘you would have been’ (ἦσθα the imperfect of εἰμί), and ὧδ’ ἀΐδηλος is ‘so destructive’. ἐνέρτερος is the comparative ‘lower, further down’, with the genitive Οὐρανιώνων ‘the sons of Uranus’ (Οὐρανός is Heaven); these are usually understood to be the Titans, the old gods held below the earth. Zeus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, καὶ Παιήον’ ἀνώγειν ἰήσασθαι.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, kai Paiēon’ anōgein iēsasthai.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Paieon he bade to heal him.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and bade Paieon heal him.
sentences.n: The subject is Zeus. ἀνώγειν is the epic pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’ (a perfect with present sense), used as an imperfect: ‘he bade’; Παιήον’ is the elided accusative of Paieon, the healer of the gods. ἰήσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἰάομαι ‘heal’, and Ares is the one to be healed, understood.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Παιήων ὀδυνήφατα φάρμακα πάσσων
ἠκέσατ’·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ epi Paiēōn odynēphata pharmaka passōn
ēkesat’·
sentences.l:
And upon him Paieon, sprinkling pain-slaying drugs,
healed him;
sentences.i: Paieon sprinkled pain-killing drugs on him and healed him;
sentences.n: The line is 5.401, where Paieon heals Hades after Heracles’ arrow, and the English is the same. τῷ δ’ ἐπί … πάσσων is ‘upon him … sprinkling’, with ἐπί split from the participle, and ὀδυνήφατα φάρμακα are ‘pain-slaying drugs’ (ὀδύνη ‘pain’, with a second half meaning ‘slaying’). ἠκέσατ’ is the elided aorist of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι καταθνητός γ’ ἐτέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti katathnētos g’ etetykto.
sentences.l: for in no way subject to death had he been made.
sentences.i: for he had not been made liable to death at all.
sentences.n: The reason a god can be healed is the one given for Hades at 5.402, where the line has τέτυκτο without the augment; here it is ἐτέτυκτο, and the English is the same. οὐ μὲν γάρ τι is ‘for not at all’, καταθνητός is ‘subject to death’ (a different word from βροτός ‘mortal’), and ἐτέτυκτο the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ὀπὸς γάλα λευκὸν ἐπειγόμενος συνέπηξεν
ὑγρὸν ἐόν, μάλα δ’ ὦκα περιτρέφεται κυκόωντι,
ὣς ἄρα καρπαλίμως ἰήσατο θοῦρον Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ opos gala leukon epeigomenos synepēxen
hygron eon, mala d’ ōka peritrephetai kykoōnti,
hōs ara karpalimōs iēsato thouron Arēa.
sentences.l:
And as when fig-juice, pressing on, curdles white milk,
being liquid, and very quickly it thickens for the one stirring,
so then swiftly he healed impetuous Ares.
sentences.i: As when fig-juice, working fast, curdles white milk, liquid as it is, and it thickens very quickly for the one who stirs it, so swiftly did he heal impetuous Ares.
sentences.n: A comparison: ὡς … ὣς ‘as … so’. ὀπός is plant juice, and the fig’s is meant (it is the usual curdler of milk; the fig is not named here). ἐπειγόμενος is ‘pressing on, working fast’, and συνέπηξεν is the aorist of συμπήγνυμι ‘fasten together, curdle’, an aorist that states what always happens. ὑγρὸν ἐόν is ‘though it is liquid’, περιτρέφεται ‘thickens’ in the present, and κυκόωντι the dative participle of κυκάω ‘stir’, ‘for the one stirring’. θοῦρον Ἄρηα ‘impetuous Ares’ keeps the stock epithet.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἥβη λοῦσεν, χαρίεντα δὲ εἵματα ἕσσε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ Hēbē lousen, charienta de heimata hesse·
sentences.l: And him Hebe bathed, and graceful clothes put on him;
sentences.i: Hebe bathed him and dressed him in graceful clothes;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ is Ares. Ἥβη is Hebe, the goddess who fitted Hera’s chariot at 5.722. λοῦσεν is the aorist of λούω ‘bathe’, and ἕσσε the unaugmented aorist of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, which takes εἵματα ‘clothes’ and the adjective χαρίεντα ‘graceful’.

sentences.t: πὰρ δὲ Διὶ Κρονίωνι καθέζετο κύδεϊ γαίων.
sentences.tr: par de Dii Kroniōni kathezeto kydeï gaiōn.
sentences.l: and beside Zeus, the son of Cronus, he sat down, exulting in glory.
sentences.i: and he sat down beside Zeus, the son of Cronus, exulting in his glory.
sentences.n: The first half-line is the one used at 869, where Ares sat down grieving; the repeated words show how his state has changed. κύδεϊ γαίων is ‘exulting in glory’ (γαίων the participle of γαίω ‘exult’), the same words as at 1.405.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ αὖτις πρὸς δῶμα Διὸς μεγάλοιο νέοντο
Ἥρη τ’ Ἀργείη καὶ Ἀλαλκομενηῒς Ἀθήνη
παύσασαι βροτολοιγὸν Ἄρη’ ἀνδροκτασιάων.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ autis pros dōma Dios megaloio neonto
Hērē t’ Argeiē kai Alalkomenēïs Athēnē
pausasai brotoloigon Arē’ androktasiaōn.
sentences.l:
And they, back again, to the house of great Zeus returned,
Argive Hera and Alalcomenean Athena,
having made mortal-ruining Ares cease from man-slayings.
sentences.i: And they went back to the house of great Zeus, Argive Hera and Alalcomenean Athena, having stopped Ares, the ruin of mortals, from his man-slayings.
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are Hera and Athena, named in 908; νέοντο is the imperfect of νέομαι ‘go, return’, and αὖτις ‘back again’. Ἥρη τ’ Ἀργείη καὶ Ἀλαλκομενηῒς Ἀθήνη is the line that names the two goddesses at 4.8, with the same English. παύσασαι is the feminine aorist participle of παύω ‘make cease’, with the accusative βροτολοιγὸν Ἄρη’ (Ἄρηα) and the genitive ἀνδροκτασιάων ‘from man-slayings’.
